claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
Differences in constituent-element diffusivities during cooling cause local compositional segregation.
Local compositional segregation triggers nucleation of ordered phases from the high-temperature BCC state.
The segregation is expected to involve Al or Cr especially.
Nanoscale compositional inhomogeneities foster short-range ordering.
Nanoscale compositional inhomogeneities act as nucleation sites for new ordered phases.
Slow cooling and intermediate-temperature holds provide sufficient atomic mobility for compositional fluctuations to develop and grow.
Growth of local compositional fluctuations lowers the nucleation barrier for ordered-phase formation.
The ordered products may include B2 or sigma-type phases.
Rapid quenching suppresses significant segregation and retains a largely disordered BCC state.
Relative to rapidly quenched samples, slowly cooled and isothermally held samples should display additional diffraction signatures such as superlattice reflections.
Slowly cooled and isothermally held samples should show TEM and EDS evidence of ordered phases associated with local segregation.
Rapidly quenched samples should be compositionally more uniform and show less ordering contrast than slowly cooled and held samples.
The rapidly quenched baseline preserves the high-temperature BCC structure with negligible elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies when temperature and time are sufficient for significant atomic diffusion and local segregation.
The proposed mechanism should not operate under extreme quenching conditions.
The proposed mechanism should not operate at very low temperatures or under other conditions that inhibit diffusion.
